en: *Fanggui*, Fascicle One, Part One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhiyan of Zhixiang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan.
This sūtra originally consists of one hundred thousand verses in the foreign [language]. Formerly, the Jin-period Daoist Zhi Falin...

This [text] of thirty-six thousand stanzas was obtained from the kingdom of Khotan. On the tenth day of the third month in the year of the Chunchu fire (the *chunhuo* year) during the fourteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, at Xie Sijiang Temple in Yangzhou, the Indian Dhyāna Master Buddhabhadra held the Sanskrit manuscript in his hand and translated the foreign sounds into the Jin language. The Śramaṇa Shi Faye personally received the transcription from the pen. At that time, Meng Yi, the Interior Historian of Wu Commandery, and Chu Shudu, General of the Right Guard, served as the patrons (*dānapati*).

It was completed on the tenth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Yuanxi era, based on the Hu (Central Asian) manuscript; it was finalized after collation on the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month in the year of Xinyou, the second year of the Yongchu era of the Taizong dynasty.
Now, in analyzing the meaning of the text, it is distinguished by way of five sections:

first, praising the virtuous capacity and the resulting state of the Sage as he approaches the occasion; second, clarifying the classification and boundaries of the scriptural collections (*piṭaka*); third, discerning the fundamental tenets and purport of what is explained by the teaching, as well as the essential nature of the teaching that explains them; fourth, interpreting the title of the sutra; and fifth, explaining the divisions of the text.

First, regarding the praise of the Sage’s virtue and capacity as he responds to the opportune moment: when the Great Sage Tathāgata first realized the profound traces for himself, he set forth from the state of non-abiding;
his spirit was harmonized with wondrous stillness, and his resolve was exalted toward Bodhi.

Thus, one is able to plant the seeds of the Way at the prior limit, accumulate virtuous karma within non-self, polish the wheel of right wisdom upon the diamond-like mind, and illuminate suchness within the realm of objects. Therefore, although delusive thoughts are not severed, one soars beyond the mundane; though the spiritual mirror is not polished, its perfect clarity constitutes equal enlightenment. In profound stillness, the self is pure and nothing remains hidden; in the concentration of traces, eternal bliss is bestowed everywhere. Birth-and-death and nirvana are viewed with equal equanimity; virtue is fully perfected, great wisdom is unobstructed, and the wondrous culmination of liberation and skillful means is thus realized.
Second, regarding the delimitation of what is subsumed within the *pitaka*: How could this profound stillness be contained within words?

Yet, because Great Compassion descends to provide instruction without any private or hidden intent, there arise teachings that accord with conditions; since the dharma-gates are not one and the distinct teachings are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, how could one possibly limit their scope with the eyes?
To distinguish them according to their categories, there are three teaching gates regarding the beginning and end of a single transformation:
first, the Gradual Teaching; second, the Sudden Teaching; and third, the Perfect Teaching.
Because there are three meanings expounded within the initial gate of the gradual [teaching], the teachings themselves are threefold.
Because there are two types of intended purpose, the teachings are likewise twofold.
As for the threefold classification:

the first is called *sūtra*, which is translated here as "thread" (*sūtra*) and is also termed "discourse" (*jing*). This is because a thread can string together flowers, and a discourse can hold together the warp; their functional meanings are thus analogous.

However, because this region values the title of the sūtra itself and does not prize the name of the translator, the translation followed what was valued; thus, the translator's name was omitted and only the title of the sūtra was retained.

Just as the holy teachings are able to penetrate the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), preventing their loss or distortion and ensuring that the Dharma endures for a long time, the Sūtra is similar to a thread;
this name is established based on this analogy, and it refers to the teaching that elucidates meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Second is *vinaya*, which here is translated as "extinguishing" (*mie*). Because the evils of body, speech, and mind incinerate the practitioner—its meaning being identical to that of a blazing fire—the precepts are able to extinguish them; thus it is called "extinguishing. This name is designated based on its functional efficacy.
The teaching, insofar as it is that which is expounded, is also called "cessation"; this refers specifically to the teaching on the precepts.
Third is Abhidharma, which is translated here as "Incomparable Dharma" (Anupama-dharma) and is also termed "Dharma in Conjunction" (Abhimukha-dharma).

It is able to destroy afflictions and the conceptualization of dharmas; non-conceptual wisdom is the most supreme, and there is no other dharma that can be compared to it; therefore, it is called "the incomparable dharma" (anupama-dharma), which derives its name from the fact that there is nothing else like it.
The teaching, by virtue of that which it elucidates, is also called the "Incomparable Dharma" (*anupamadharmā*); this refers specifically to the teaching that elucidates wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is termed "Abhidharma" because *abhi* signifies the "confronting wisdom" and *dharma* signifies the "object confronted," thus establishing the name based on the function of the object.
These latter two Piṭakas both derive their names from what they expound.
Question:
If this is so, why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state: "The Sūtra-piṭaka is established separately for the sake of teaching the three types of training"?
"To establish the training that relies on morality and the training that relies on the mind, the Vinaya was instituted.
Based on this textual evidence, it follows that the Sūtras elucidate three types of conduct, the Vinaya elucidates two types of conduct, and the Abhidharma elucidates one type of conduct.
Answer: There are two meanings: first, the door of defining the essential nature; second, the door of including both the primary and secondary.
The defining of the essential nature is as previously explained.
Furthermore, "correcting the gate" has two meanings:
first, the meaning of root and branch.
The Sūtras constitute the fundamental teaching, while the other two [the Vinaya and Abhidharma] are successively its branches.
The second is the combined approach of the correct gates.
In the Sūtras, concentration is established as the correct [gate], while precepts and wisdom are combined.
The same applies to the Vinaya and the Śāstras; this may be understood by analogy.
This sutra is subsumed within the Sūtra-piṭaka.

Because there are two [types of practitioners], the teaching is likewise twofold: since faculties are either sharp or dull and dharmas are either shallow or profound, the three piṭakas are established based on the dull faculties of the śrāvakas, in order to perfect the dharmas of the śrāvaka practice.

For Bodhisattvas of sharp faculties, the three baskets (tripiṭaka) are established based on the meaning of the three non-natures, such as the non-discriminative nature, in order to accomplish the dharmas of Bodhisattva practice.
Question:
The Sūtra says, "For the sake of the various Pratyekabuddhas, he taught the method of contemplating dependent origination."
If there is also a teaching for pratyekabuddhas, why is a separate piṭaka not established for them?
Answer: According to the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*, the teachings of the three vehicles are established as the three piṭakas.

Now, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, those who merely rely on provisional teachings enter the Śrāvaka Piṭaka; therefore, they are not established [as a separate vehicle].
This is clarified by two points:

first, the "Śrāvaka-śrāvaka" refers to one who originally sought the path of the śrāvaka and delighted in contemplating the Four Noble Truths, and who now encounters the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and thereby attains the Way.
Because they previously possessed the spiritual lineage and now further hear the sound [of the Dharma], they are called "Hearers of Sound" (śrāvaka).
As it is said in the Sūtra: "For those who seek the state of a śrāvaka, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths."

Based on this statement, regarding the two types—the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas—they previously sought the path of a Pratyekabuddha, but now encounter the Buddha’s teaching on the doctrine of causes and conditions.
As it is said in the sūtras: "For those who seek the state of a Pratyekabuddha, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination."
Regarding this, we shall discuss it as follows:

the former sense refers to the knowledge of phenomena through their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), while the latter sense refers to the knowledge of phenomena through their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Although they differ in terms of sharp or dull faculties, both aim for the same minor fruit; thus, taken together, they constitute one Piṭaka.

If those of superior faculties appear in an age without a Buddha, they realize the causes and conditions through self-awakening and attain the fruit of the Way; since there is practice but no teaching, [the latter] is set aside based on this.
According to the *Puyao jing* (Lalitavistara Sūtra), this distinguishes between principle and teaching.

Among the Śrāvakas, there are two types: namely, those who adhere to the teachings on the nature of grasping (*grāhaka-svabhāva*), and those who follow the teachings on the nature of refutation (*bhaṅga-svabhāva*).

As for the teachings on the nature of refutation, they understand the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and, likewise relying upon the Four Noble Truths, proceed toward the minor fruit; therefore, they are included within the Śrāvaka Piṭaka.
Second, regarding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, there are two internal categories:
first, those who previously practiced the Great Dharma but later regressed and entered the Lesser Vehicle, and now return to advance toward the Great Vehicle.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Except for those who have previously cultivated and studied the Hīnayāna, I shall now also cause them to enter this Dharma."
This is called "gradual entry.
Second, those who have long practiced the Mahāyāna and only now see the Buddha are able to enter [the path] suddenly.

Thus, the Sūtra says: "There are sentient beings who, throughout successive lifetimes, have always received my transformation; as soon as they see my body and hear what I preach, they immediately believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
This sutra is thus included within the Mahāyāna teachings.

Second, regarding its inclusion within the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*), the subsequent sutra states: "If there are sentient beings of inferior capacity whose minds are weary and despondent, he shows them the path of the Śrāvaka to enable them to emerge from all sufferings."
Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose faculties are slightly clear and sharp, who delight in the Dharma of causes and conditions; for them, he preaches the path of the Pratyekabuddha.
If there are persons whose faculties are clear and sharp, who benefit sentient beings, and possess a heart of great compassion, for them he preaches the Bodhisattva path.
"If there are those with the unsurpassed mind who are determinedly delighted by the Great Matter, for their sake I manifest the Buddha-body and preach the immeasurable Buddha-dharmas.
Based on this textual evidence, we know that there is a distinction between the One Vehicle and the Sudden Teaching of the Three Vehicles.
Furthermore, according to Paramārtha’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*:
first, the One Vehicle; second, the Three Vehicles; and third, the Lesser Vehicle.
Question:
What distinguishes sudden enlightenment from the One Vehicle? Answer:
This is not fixed; they may be indistinguishable, or they may be distinguished according to wisdom and teaching.
Furthermore, there is one that is shallow and one that is deep; the One Vehicle Treasury (Ekayāna-piṭaka) corresponds to the ten treasuries mentioned below.
Their mutual inclusion should be understood by analogy.

Regarding the third, the "Perfect Teaching" (Yuanjiao): for those who have attained a partial stage of the Buddha’s realm, it expounds the dharma-gate of ultimate liberation and fulfills the Buddha-work; therefore, it is called "Perfect."
This sutra is subsumed under both the Sudden and Perfect teachings.

That there is a Perfect teaching is known from the passage in the text below which says, "Just as because of the great ocean there are ten jewel mountains," and so forth; one should judge accordingly.
Question:
For what reason has this sutra, up to this point, been explained through the distinctions and subsumptions of the three vehicles? Answer:
The primary tenet of this sutra comprises both the common and the distinct teachings, as it encompasses the objects, views, hearing, and practice of the three vehicles.

This is illustrated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where within the triple world, the three carts are used to lead the children out of the house, and upon reaching the open space, the great ox-cart is bestowed individually.
Furthermore, these two teachings alike exist within the triple world as objects of sight and hearing.

Moreover, since those such as the śrāvakas are like "poor sons" who are led by [the Buddha], we know that apart from the Hīnayāna there are separately three vehicles; they mutually lead one another, forming a system of principal and attendant.
The section on the classification of the contents is concluded.
Third, regarding the explanation of the tenets and ultimate goals elucidated by the teaching below, there are two types:
first, the general; second, the specific.
In general, it is said that the principle of dependent origination regarding cause and effect is the actual thesis and purport.
Specifically, there are four gates:

first, distinguishing the thesis and purport by correlating the teaching with its meaning; second, the object and the practice; third, the phenomenon and the principle; and fourth, the cause and the effect.

The teaching is the primary focus and the meaning is the goal; the object is the primary focus and the practice is the goal; the phenomenon is the primary focus and the principle is the goal; the cause is the primary focus and the fruit is the goal.
Next, regarding the nature of the teaching that expresses [the meaning], there are five types:
first, the actual sounds, names, phrases, and syllables;
second, those that resemble sounds, names, phrases, and syllables.
The third meaning is that names, phrases, and syllables do not resemble sounds;
the fourth meaning is that names, phrases, and syllables are merely consciousness;
the fifth meaning is that names, phrases, and syllables are *tathatā* (suchness); therefore, the Sūtra says, "All phenomena are like [suchness]."

1. Chapter on the Pure Eye of the World: An Explanation of the Title of the Scripture. Regarding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*, the "Chapter on the Pure Eye of the World": "Great" (*mahā*) refers to the fact that its essence, attributes, and functions are unsurpassed. This means its essence is one of equality, neither increasing nor decreasing; its attributes are the complete fulfillment of the qualities of nature; and its function is the production of the causes and effects of both mundane and supramundane goodness.
"Square" (fang) means that the principle is correct and not erroneous.
"Vast" (guang) means that the dharma-gates, principles, and numerical categories fully possess all virtues to their ultimate limit.
"Buddha" (fo) means awakening; this term encompasses the ten Buddhas as well as the Buddhas of the three bodies (trikāya).
There are two kinds of flowers:
first, those that produce fruit but do not coexist with it, such as the practice of the path within saṃsāra, and so forth, up to the roots of goodness during the stage of a cause.

The two types of adornments—the flowers and the fruits—arise simultaneously with the fruits themselves, such as the flowers of the seven purities (*sapta-viśuddhi*) and the various virtues of the stage of perfected fruition (*phala-avasthā*).
It should be understood that those produced through cultivation and those innate from the beginning mutually adorn one another.
"Exalted" (*yán*) means adorned and embellished.
Furthermore, the term "Great" (*dà*) is used as a supreme designation for its preeminence. Thus, the Treatise states:

"Great," "Victorious," "High," and "Vast" are one in essence yet differ in name. The intent of this vehicle is rich and profound; it encompasses all things without exception, and is therefore called the Great Root (*Dàběn*).
It is not merely a matter of being square.

To speak of "square" refers to the ultimate state of perfect penetration; it is to be well-situated in all circumstances, to accord with conditions whenever encountered, and to bestow without discrimination—therefore, it is called "square."

As for the term "vast" (*guǎng*): it is profound and mysterious, subtle and far-reaching, deep and extensive; thus it is called "vast. As for the term "Buddha": the correct pronunciation in the Middle Kingdom is *bútuó*;

here in this land, he is called a "Wakened One" (*juézhě*). Because he has attained clarity and reached the ultimate source, his habitual defilements have forever vanished; because he harbors luminous, solitary brilliance that illuminates the great night and guides the masses of delusion, awakening himself and awakening others, he is therefore called *Buddha*.

As for the term "Avataṃsaka," it is a metaphor for the excellence of the virtues of the Dharmakāya’s practice. Thus, were its essence not truly real, there would be no way to manifest its subtlety; were its merit not ultimate, there would be no way to reveal its supremacy. As they mutually illuminate one another, their meanings are both transcendent and extraordinary; it may indeed be called the ultimate pinnacle of self-existent, perfect, pervasive, and sublime excellence.

It is like a golden countenance exquisitely adorned with various silks and rare jewels, surpassingly magnificent and peerless in the world; thus, based on this analogy, it is given its name and called the *Avataṃsaka*.

The *sūtra* is the teaching of true purity; it instructs on eternal norms, with its prose as the warp and its principles as the woof, manifesting the application of the mind in practice; hence it is called a *sūtra*.
"The pure eye of the world" refers to the three worlds, such as the time, the vessel, and the sentient beings.

Furthermore, there is the characteristic of that which performs the comparison, as well as the distinction between essence and function; thus, the present world is unimpeded and unstained, serving as a comparison for the pure eye.
It may also be said that before the Tathāgata appeared in the world, beings were like the blind because they lacked a virtuous guide;
now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, he manifests the purity of both self and others, serving as a metaphor for having clear eyes and ears.

Regarding the term "Pure Eye of the World," this should properly be called the introduction; however, those present at this current assembly are all *śrāvakas* who have entered the ocean-like multitude of the Buddha’s followers. Their virtue abides in the pure realm, untainted by worldly dust, and they have emerged from the natural state (*tianzhen*), their faith being truly non-conditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, [the teaching] relies upon them to manifest the subtlety of the ultimate, perfect path of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): not abandoning birth and death yet remaining unstained. For this reason, it is designated according to its function, hence it is called the "Pure Eye of the World."
It is difficult to fathom; it cannot be understood except through metaphors, which are thus established to approximate its form.
If the eye is pure both internally and externally, and its interior and exterior are transparently clear, such that forms and images are arrayed therein, all belong to a single movement.
Being neither small nor large, neither distant nor near, they do not obstruct one another; thus, by way of analogy, it may be designated as being "like the eye.
Therefore, the subsequent verse praises it, saying: "The world is pure, just like the eye. The meaning clearly confirms that the holy teaching is indeed so.
Regarding "fascicle" (*pin*): when linguistic expressions and principles are uniform, and categories are grouped together, they are designated as a "fascicle.
This sutra contains thirty-four fascicles; as this particular fascicle runs through the beginning of the entire work, it is called the "First."

The general overview of the sutra and the circumstances of its essential tenets have their meaning clarified herein; therefore, it is called the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the Great Vaipulya Scripture of the Buddha.
Fifth, regarding the word-by-word commentary: first is the general summary and analysis of the scope of the teaching;
second is the specific explanation of the divisions of the text, which has two parts:
First, distinguishing the boundaries by contrasting with what is erroneous; second, distinguishing the boundaries according to the meaning expressed.
Regarding the first—distinguishing by contrasting with what is erroneous—there are four sections:
first, distinguishing error in terms of conditions, such as the eight occasions when speech is improper.
Second, it is explained in terms of karma: for instance, seeking fame and profit, asserting one's own views while disparaging others, and delighting in worldly existence, and so forth.

Third, it is clarified in terms of afflictions (*kleśa*): hearing and yet misunderstanding what was heard, failing to hear what should have been heard, and even [misapplying] such principles as "rely on the Dharma, not on the person," and so forth.
Fourth, distinguishing [the nature of] error by way of beginning and end, as the Sūtra says: "The eight great virtuous persons and others shall become non-virtuous.
Second, clarifying the boundaries by way of what is expressed, there are briefly ten gates:
first, the gate of simultaneous, complete, and corresponding manifestation.

Within this, there are ten [perfections]: first, the perfection of both teaching and meaning; second, the perfection of both principle and phenomena; third, the perfection of both understanding and practice; fourth, the perfection of both cause and effect; fifth, the perfection of both person and dharma; sixth, the perfection of the boundaries, objects, and stages; seventh, the perfection of both teacher and disciple, and dharma and wisdom; eighth, the perfection of both principal and attendant, and basis and manifestation; ninth, the perfection of mastery over both the inverse and the direct, and essence and function; tenth, the perfection of manifesting in accordance with the faculties and desires of sentient beings.
These ten gates are mutually interrelated and possess no sequence of before or after.
Second is the gate of the *Indra’s Net* realm.
Within this, the preceding ten gates are fully contained; however, they differ only in that their meanings follow the analogy, while the rest may be inferred from what has been stated above.
3. The Door of the Simultaneous Manifestation and Concealment of the Three Mysteries.
This also possesses the ten preceding doors; however, their meanings differ according to conditions, as may be inferred from the above.
4. The Door of the Mutual Containment and Establishment of the Subtle.
This [gate] also possesses the ten preceding sections; it differs from them only in that its meaning is based on "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), while the rest may be inferred accordingly.

The gate of the "differentiation of dharmas separated by fifty worlds" (*pañcāśad-loka-vyavahita-dharma-bheda-siddhi-mukha*) also possesses the ten preceding sections; it differs from them only in that its meaning is based on "worlds" (*loka*), while the rest may be inferred accordingly.
Sixth, the gate of the various treasuries being pure, mixed, and endowed with merit:
this also possesses the ten preceding gates; however, the meaning differs according to the world [of discourse], and the rest may be inferred accordingly.
Seventh, the gate of the mutual containment of the one and the many without confusion.
This also possesses the ten preceding gates; however, the meaning differs from that [of the previous gate] in terms of principle (*li*).
The remainder may be inferred accordingly. Eighth is the Gate of the Mutual Identity and Sovereignty of All Dharmas.

This also possesses the ten preceding gates; however, the meaning differs from that [of the previous gate] in terms of function (*yong*). The remainder may be inferred accordingly, or it may also be based on nature (*xing*).
Ninth is the gate of the excellent accomplishment of the revolution of mind-only.
This also possesses the ten preceding gates; however, the meaning differs insofar as it proceeds from the mind, and the others may be inferred accordingly.
Tenth is the gate of generating understanding by relying on phenomena to reveal the Dharma.
This [teaching] also possesses the ten preceding gates; however, it differs from them solely in its meaning as derived from wisdom. The remainder may be inferred accordingly.

Among the ten profound gates above, each is distinct; if the demarcation of the teachings and their meanings corresponds with this, they constitute the Perfect Teaching and the Sudden Teaching of the One Vehicle.
If various demarcations of teachings and meanings correspond with this but are not fully complete, they are subsumed under the Gradual Teaching of the Three Vehicles.
The remaining meanings may be understood by referring to the subsequent Dharma-gates concerning the Heavenly Kings and others;

they can be explained accordingly. Regarding the word-by-word commentary: first, eight types of teachings are briefly cited to clarify their mutual formation, followed by an explanation of their sequence based on the three teachings; subsequently, the text is interpreted passage by passage.

Regarding these eight teachings: first, the demarcation between the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles; second, the True and the Responsive; third, the transformation of the three into one; fourth, emptiness and existence; fifth, the mutual dependence of the ordinary and the sage; sixth, permanence and impermanence; seventh, the common practice of the three vehicles; and eighth, the discernment of the heterodox and the orthodox.

These eight meanings apply throughout both the preceding and following sections. Whether explained extensively or concisely, they mutually support one another to establish the two aspects of the fundamental and the derivative;

these should be considered accordingly. Regarding the establishment of the three teachings: it refers to the beginning at the Bodhi tree, where for the sake of those of great practice, the ultimate essence of the school was presented directly and straightforwardly. The Dharma-wheel of Vaipulya is profound and mysterious in its intent, requiring no further mediation; thus, it is designated as "Sudden."

What is called "gradual" refers to the establishment of skillful means for those who first begin their practice; it is the transformative teaching that develops and guides through the three vehicles. Beginning subtly and ending with clarity, proceeding from the shallow to the deep, one ascends by stages upon successive vehicles to reach the other shore; therefore, it is termed "gradual."

As for what is called the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): it refers to the teaching of the Tathāgata’s dharma-gate of liberation for those who have reached the higher stages and partially attained the realm of the Buddha; because it exhausts the ultimate principle and reaches the most supreme fruit-practice, fulfilling all Buddha-works, it is therefore called "Perfect."
If one investigates this through its reality, the ultimate convergence is non-dual; it is equalized as a single flavor, exhaustive and without remainder. What difference could there be?

It is only because the functions of their respective remedies are unequal that the teachings are distinguished as shallow or deep according to the capacities of sentient beings, such that we speak of three divisions.

Regarding their sequence: based on the definitive and ultimate teaching of the One Vehicle, and according to the distinctions between the skillful means of counteraction and the various gateways of practice, there are three essential points that clarify the sequence:

First, by relying on the relative counteractions cultivated through skillful means and the causal practices of dependent origination within their own respective categories, the three teachings are elucidated. "Gradual" (Jian) is placed first, "Sudden" (Dun) in the middle, and "Perfect" (Yuan) last. These three meanings are explained from the perspective of the gradual: first, the gradual is used to engender faith; next, the sudden is used to establish practice; and finally, the perfect is used to perfect the essence and function.

If we explain the temporal sequence by means of the causal practice of the actual reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the nature of dependent origination, there are three stages: sudden at the beginning, gradual in the middle, and perfect at the end. This is because, first, the sudden is shown to inspire practice; next, the gradual is shown to manifest for the sake of sentient beings; and finally, the perfect fruit is shown as the fullness of merit.

If one considers the stage of the profound and secret resultant path—the very essence of unobstructed dependent origination that neither increases nor decreases when fully exhausting the reality-dharmadhātu—then there is first the Perfect [Teaching], followed by the Sudden, and finally the Gradual.

The reason for this is that the profound principle does not exclude those of subtle contemplation, and the perfect Way does not discriminate against those at the initial stage of entry. Therefore, although the matters are near, they reach the farthest; although the signs are manifest, they reach the most subtle. Only when the shallow reaches the ultimate depth can one exhaustively realize them. Thus, first the Perfect [Teaching] is shown so that they may see and hear it; next the Sudden [Teaching] is revealed so that they may rejoice in accordance with it; and finally the gradual stages are distinguished to manifest its virtues, thereby giving rise to faith and practice.
This is simply an explanation of the three [bodies] by way of the Perfect [Body].

While this may be so regarding the teaching (*śāsana*), when we examine its underlying principle (*artha*), it correctly elucidates the unsurpassed *bodhi* of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body—the ultimate, perfect path that accords with and exhausts the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Its virtues overflow from the depths of the ocean; its meaning arises from the true source and illuminates the future limit. It expresses the fruit through non-attainment and clarifies the cause through non-arising. Thus, the characteristic of the signless is profound and subtle; it coalesces with the great void, its principle transcending names and forms. One might say that while the ultimate Way is wordless, the profound scriptures are extensively spread; while the true countenance is formless, the wondrous marks are fully adorned. Entering the Buddha-wisdom and possessing the Buddha’s conduct, its manifest virtue is exceptionally beautiful, surpassing all worldly things.

Therefore, the reason the beginning of this sutra is permeated with the title "Buddha-Flower Adornment" (Avataṃsaka) should be understood according to the explanation of Master Zhinan; the essential core of its doctrine resides therein.
As for the word-by-word commentary, this single body of teaching is broadly divided into three parts:
namely, the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination.
If one were to analyze this vertically, there are ten distinct meanings corresponding to its eight assemblies; the rest may be understood by analogy.
This single scripture consists of seven locations and eight assemblies: three held among humans and four in the heavens, which constitute the "seven locations";
the repeated assembly at the Universal Radiance (Samantābhāsvara) constitutes the "eighth assembly."
This constitutes the sequential method of the stages; thus, there are only seven or eight [assemblies].
Regarding these seven or eight, the textual characteristics differ in terms of presence or absence, which will be briefly analyzed through ten categories.

Within the eight assemblies, the reason the Buddha is elucidated first is that the Buddha is the principal teacher of transformation; since the present gathering of sentient beings must necessarily prioritize the principal teacher of transformation, he is elucidated at the outset.
Second, regarding the two Great Sages preaching the Dharma, there is that upon which they rely; next, the location is distinguished.
Third, regarding the sphere of conversion and guidance, next the Bodhisattvas are clarified.
Fourth, although the vessel [of the listener] is fully endowed, if the request is not complete, the teaching will not be given; therefore, doubt subsequently arises.
The five dharmas provide boundless moisture; next, the gathering of new assemblies is distinguished.
Sixth, because subtle dharmas are not easily scrutinized and cannot be explained immediately, the entry into meditative concentration is distinguished next.
Seventh, wishing to distinguish the excellence of the Dharma, the Buddha’s empowerment is clarified.
Eighth, the section clarifies the limits of the Dharma from its beginning to its end; next, it explains the distinction between those who have emerged [from the womb] and those who have not.
Ninth, once the supreme Dharma has been proclaimed, it next clarifies the benefits of the Dharma; therefore, it describes such events as the shaking of the earth and the raining of flowers.

Tenth, since the efficacy has been manifested and the transformation is neither partial nor biased, the turning [of the Dharma wheel] throughout the ten directions is simultaneous and harmonious, without fail; therefore, next, the equality of the synthesis is distinguished, manifesting realization and completing the exposition.
If these ten are separated from the "raining of flowers" and so forth, there would be fifteen.
The scattering of flowers, burning of incense, emitting light, performing music, and raining jewels—these five are subsumed into one; thus, they are all now included within the ten.
Second, regarding the paired explanation of existence and non-existence: among the three bodies of the Buddha in the seven locations, which one is it?
There are two ways of explaining this:
first, the specific (particular), and second, the general.
Regarding the "locale" (*sthāna*): since all eight assemblies are not of limited views, it is therefore the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Question:
Since the *saṃbhogakāya* is not a *nirmāṇakāya*, why is its location the same as that of the latter?
Answer: This was done because he first transformed beings who were drifting toward the end times; thus, he distinguished them by means of their worldly stations.
Furthermore, it is asked:
If one abides in the world, why does the sutra state that it is "accomplished" in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven?
Answer: There are two meanings to this.
First, relying on the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) to manifest the retribution body, which refers to the eight assemblies;
second, relying on the retribution body to manifest the transformation body, which refers to the ultimate limit of form (*rūpa-paryanta*).
To demonstrate that the desire realm is a transformation, it is stated that its characteristics are transformations; this is merely to clarify the intent of the teaching in the present discussion.
As for "pervasion," it means that the three bodies are fully present, each mutually constituting the others.

This is known from the passage in the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra* which states, "Within my body there is no obstruction," as well as from the descriptions of the Flower Treasury World-Ocean (*Huāzàng Shìjièhǎi*) and the allegorical references to the Bodhi tree and so forth.
This is distinguished according to the Three Vehicles;
if distinguished according to the One Vehicle, then all ten Buddhas mentioned below are universally present.
As for the division of the text into three parts, they are the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Circulation.
The introduction consists of the characteristics of skillful means; the main body explains the characteristics of the essence; and the dissemination concerns the characteristics of its utility.
This "Chapter on the Pure Eye" constitutes the introduction, while from the "Vairocana" chapter downward, the orthodox teaching is elucidated.
Because the sutra has not been fully transmitted, there is no complete circulation [of it].
This is known from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states: "The inconceivable sutra consists of one hundred thousand verses, whereas this version contains only thirty-six thousand verses."
Thus it is known. There may also be a section on circulation, which begins from the passage "the mind of sentient beings is like a microdust" and so forth.
However, because Master Nāgārjuna, for the sake of the assembly and other locations, abridged the hundred thousand [verse version] to its present form, it is insufficient.
If one were to distinguish them according to the literal meaning of the text, they would be analyzed separately in the text itself.
The introductory section is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the *śraddhā-prasāda* (faith and confidence); second, from "The Heavenly Kings presented offerings," etc., the explanation of the *nidāna* (introductory narrative).
The Preface of Certification and Faith has two meanings:
the first two lines of four characters apply specifically to this certification and faith;
from "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) onwards, the meaning is general.
This refers to a single meaning alone.
Furthermore, it is also possible for the meaning of two phrases to pervade the entire treatise while the phrasing remains restricted;
whereas from the initial phrase "At one time" onwards, the phrasing pervades [the text] while the meaning remains restricted.
Based on this meaning, there are six points:
first, "Thus"; second, "I have heard"; third, "at one time"; fourth, "the Buddha"; fifth, "the dwelling place"; and sixth, "the assembly of listeners."
First, regarding the explanation of "Thus" (evam): it is because the principles and teachings of the various sages correspond in both letter and meaning.
Alternatively, it may mean that the letter and meaning transmitted by me are just as they were spoken by the Buddha.
This is the meaning of the holy teaching.
Furthermore, it is merely words of faithful compliance.
"Thus have I heard" can be understood accordingly.
"At one time" refers to the moment when the faculties and the teaching are in accord.
There are three meanings of "time":
first, the time of equanimity, meaning there is neither sinking nor agitation, and no inversion.
Second, at the time of their conjunction, it means causing the listener to hear, be able to hear, and hear correctly.
Third, at the time of turning the wheel of Dharma, it means correct preaching and correct reception.
"Buddha" is as can be understood.
As for the "location," it refers to the site of the tranquil Way in Magadha, which is the place entrusted to the Great Sage.
Since he is present in one place, he is present in all; though the country is general, the site is specific. This is called the Kingdom of No Harm (Aṅga).
"Quiescent extinction" (*śānti*) signifies the pure and quiescent virtues of the perfected fruit that is free from hindrances.

Regarding "initially accomplished," there are two meanings: first, the beginning of attaining the Way, which occurs during the first seven days; [the second refers to the initial moment of enlightenment].

Second, the manifestation in the present world and the initial preaching of the Dharma; this refers to the second seven-day period, because it marks the point at which others came to know that he had attained enlightenment.
This passage consists of two parts:
first, the initial two lines provide a general opening by establishing the thesis regarding the primary and secondary supports (*āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*); second, the specific analysis.
The "separate internal" section is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the dependent retribution (the environment); second, from the words "The Tathāgata dwells here," the explanation of the primary retribution (the body).
The first refers to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
The text consists of three parts:
first, the identification of the site of the bodhimanda; second, from "That bodhi tree" downward, the identification of the bodhi tree;
third, from "inconceivable" downward, the elucidation of the lion throne.

Regarding this intended meaning: the ground serves as the foundation for dwelling and practice; the tree represents the establishment of manifold virtues; and the seat signifies the function of gathering and benefiting others. Within the first section, there are three sub-points:

first, distinguishing the complete adornment of the essence of the *bodhimaṇḍa*; second, clarifying the accomplishment of the qualities of fruition from the words "By the Buddha’s spiritual power" onwards; and third, revealing the causal practices from the words "Immeasurable roots of goodness" onwards.
The initial section on the essence of the text further consists of three parts:

first, a general exposition of the essence; second, six lines beginning with "various miscellaneous jewel flowers" that expound the virtues of self-benefit; and third, two lines beginning with "raining inexhaustible jewels" that expound the virtues of benefiting both oneself and others.

Among the six phrases concerning self-benefit, the first is purity of subtle, wondrous, and perfect nature; the second is purity of possessing virtues; the third is purity of physical marks; the fourth is purity of sublime manifestation; the fifth is purity of retinue; and the sixth is purity of radiant splendor.

Within the two lines concerning benefiting others: first, the purity of the function of providing passage is clarified; next, the purity of covering and moistening is clarified. These two lines apply to both self and others.
Following this, in the second sub-section beginning with "By the Buddha’s spiritual power," there are three lines:
first, the transformation of the pure land so that the ground becomes vast and expansive; second, the functional virtue beginning with "The light shines everywhere."
Third, regarding the passage beginning with "All wondrous jewels of various marvels," its essence encompasses all virtues.
Within the text concerning the Bodhi tree, there are two sections:
first, nine phrases that distinguish the adornments of the tree's substance; second, from "By the Buddha’s spiritual power" onwards, which distinguishes the accomplishment of the fruits of virtue.
The first section is divided into three parts:

first, explaining that the substance of the tree is lofty and superior, capable of providing shade; second, from "Pure lapis lazuli" onwards, five phrases correctly describe its adornments; third, from "The light of the tree shines everywhere" onwards, three phrases clarify its benefit for others, which contains three types of action: first, mental; second, physical; and third, verbal.
The section on the seat is divided into five parts:
first, clarifying that the substance of the seat transcends ordinary dimensions;
second, from "various exquisite jewel flowers" onwards, formally distinguishing its adornments.
Third, from "The flowing light is like clouds" downward, the benefit of others is distinguished; this also consists of the three karmas: first, physical; next, mental; and finally, verbal.
Fourth, from "The Tathāgata’s radiance surpasses... downward, there are five phrases concerning the superior fruit above and the empowerment below:

first, superiority in overcoming the obscuration of the aggregates; second, superiority in manifesting transformation; third, superiority in being unimpeded; fourth, superiority in rapid pervasion; and fifth, superiority in possessing virtues.
5. From "Immeasurable Multitudes of Jewels" onwards, the summary is established.
Second, the exposition of the primary retribution (*vipāka*) has two parts:
first, a general explanation beginning with "The place where the Tathāgata resides," etc.; second, a detailed analysis beginning with "Comprehending the three periods of time," etc.
The second part, the detailed explanation, consists of three sections:
first, the elucidation of the Dharma-body; second, from the passage "His body sits pervasively in all places of enlightenment" onwards, the elucidation of the Reward-body.
3. "Able to universally manifest before all assemblies" and below clarify his transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
This textual analysis is based on the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
If one relies on the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the tenfold essence, qualities, and functions of the Buddha are fully contained herein; this should be understood through systematic contemplation.
The initial passage concerning the Dharma-body consists of three phrases:
the first two phrases distinguish the virtue of bodily action (kāyakarman);
the subsequent two phrases, beginning with "wondrous voice pervading everywhere," clarify the virtue of vocal action (vākkarman).
3. Regarding the "Characteristics of the Equal Dharma" (*samatā-dharmalakṣaṇa*), the following three phrases distinguish the virtues of mental action (*manaskarma*).
Second, the text on the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is divided into three parts;
first, the functions of the body, which consist of four phrases:
First, the delimitation of the stages; second, knowing the faculties and conduct; third, eliminating the defilement of delusions; and fourth, generating virtues.
Second, the three phrases beginning with "universally emitting the light of the ocean of wisdom of the three periods" distinguish the vocal karma.
Third, the phrase beginning with "powers and fearlessnesses" clarifies the mental karma.
Third, the explanation of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) text: first, the bodily action (*kāyakarman*), which consists of three phrases;
second, the two phrases beginning with "thoroughly penetrating all," which refer to the mental action (*manaskarman*);
third, the two phrases beginning with "all radiance," which refer to the verbal action (*vākkarman*).
Regarding the text on verbal action, there are two parts:
first, an analysis of how the emission of light can universally manifest all meanings; second, from "The worlds of all Buddhas" onwards, an analysis of the scope of the benefits.
The sixth section concerns the assembly of those who heard together; this refers to the "world of sentient beings" (sattva-loka) and clarifies the perfect gathering of the great multitude.
This is analyzed through two gates:
first, clarifying the differences regarding the presence or absence of various assemblies; second, explaining according to the text.
There are two divisions:
first, the major and minor; second, the miscellaneous classes.
Regarding the major and minor: the seven assemblies are all major, while the eighth is both major and minor.

The reason for this is that the preceding [section] was intended to reveal the essence of the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna, while the eighth [chapter] is for entering the Dharma-realm; it universally encompasses those of the Hīnayāna to lead them into the Mahāyāna, thereby manifesting the power of human capacity.
Regarding the second category, the "miscellaneous classes," only the first and the last are listed as miscellaneous classes of spirit-kings (*śrī-deva*), while the others are omitted for brevity.

The reason is that the former serves to represent the practice of aspiring faith, which is like describing the characteristics of the myriad practices through the faith and understanding of those who accord with the *dharmadhātu*;
the latter serves to represent the perfection of virtue attained by those who, in accordance with the *dharmadhātu*, encompass the *dharmadhātu* and enter into cultivation.
Question:
If that is so, why does the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* encompass many categories while this [text] encompasses few? Answer:

That [teaching] was spoken from the perspective of the ripening of expectations and thus refers to the distant; this [teaching], however, is discussed in terms of the beginning and the proximate, which is why it can be understood.
Furthermore, since the beginning is also defined by the initial stage as its limit, it does not apply to the lower vehicles; the rest will be clarified below.
The second section, the explanation of the text, is divided into three parts:

first, the separate inclusion of thirty-four assemblies within the pure land of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body; second, from "At that time, at the Buddha’s lion throne" onwards, the inclusion of one assembly through the power of skillful means of the Dharma-body pure land; thus, in total from beginning to end, there are thirty-five assemblies.
First, a brief enumeration of the names of the assembly; second, an enumeration of their names followed by a praise of their virtues.
The first section is divided into two parts:
first, the identification of the bodhisattvas and others, clarifying the assembly gathered through unconditioned conditions.
Second, regarding the various deities and others, it clarifies that they are a collection formed through the conditions of conditioned origination (*saṃskṛta-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Below, their names are listed and their virtues praised; these may be understood by analogy.
Within the first section, the assembly of Bodhisattvas, there are three divisions:
First, the enumeration; second, the listing of the Bodhisattvas' names.
This section has three parts: first, the analysis; second, the conclusion; third, the praise of their virtues.
Regarding those who accompany [the Buddha], there are two parts:
First, they are together with a Buddha, and he speaks with them;
second, they are together in the transmission of the Dharma, and they hear it with him.
As for "Universal" (Pu): when virtue fills the dharma-realm, it is called Universal; when one is supremely compliant and harmoniously supple, it is called Worthy (Xian).
The reason why the name "Mixed" (miśra) is clarified here for the Bodhisattvas has two intentions:

first, to manifest the various worlds of inferior, coarse, subtle, and so forth; second, to manifest the many types of teachings within the introductory sequence of this assembly, which encompasses the eight subsequent assemblies. The rest may be understood accordingly.
The third section, "Praising Virtues," consists of four parts:

first, a general praise; second, a specific praise of one's own virtues (*svabhāga*), beginning with "the various pāramitās"; third, a specific analysis of the virtues for entering the realm of others (*parabhāga*), beginning with "unsurpassed wisdom and vows"; and fourth, an analysis of the sovereign power of Samantabhadra’s practices and vows to gather and transform beings, beginning with "attaining all Buddhas."
The general text is divided into two parts:
first, the phrase "all are virtuous friends" reveals the excellence of the persons;
"Vairocana" means "Extensive, Pure, and Adorned."
Second, the explanation of one's own stage (*svabhūmi*) consists of three sub-sections:

first, clarifying the practice for one's own benefit; second, from "the ocean of eloquence" onwards, clarifying the practice for the benefit of others; and third, from "abiding in the first stage" onwards, clarifying how the stages are established through practice.

Regarding the analysis of the boundaries of what is subsumed, the passage beginning with "Abiding in one stage universally subsumes all stages" and so forth, explains the essential nature [of the stages] by means of their progression through successive modes of practice until the ultimate realization of reality is reached.
In brief, there are four points:
first, because that which exists at the beginning can give rise to what follows until it reaches ultimate fulfillment, it is called "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*).
Second, although the beginning is complete, all [stages] are able to practice the conduct of the various stages; since all dharmas are without distinction, they are said to be "comprehended."
The practices thus accomplished reside solely within their own respective stages; the distinctions between superior and inferior, or higher and lower, are merely differences of clarity and obscurity.
These three are the very beginning, which encompass all the merits of the various stages; therefore, they are called "encompassing" (saṃgraha).

Fourth, it is not that they are called "comprehensions" (*saṃgraha*) because of their initial and final stages; rather, they are called "comprehensions" because the very beginning is itself the true end.
Within the section on self-benefit, there are three parts: namely, the general, the primary, and the auxiliary.
The passage on benefiting others consists of three parts:
the first distinguishes verbal action (*vākkarman*); the second, bodily action (*kāyakarman*); and the final three, beginning with "skillfully knowing," distinguish mental action (*manaskarman*).

Within this, the first refers to knowing the faculties (*indriya*), the second to knowing the principles of the Dharma (*dharmatattva*), and the third to knowing the phenomena of the world (*dharmavastu*).
The subsequent section consists of four points:

first, the five points clarifying self-benefit, which are: first, attaining aspiration; second, attaining instruction; third, attaining the dharma of fruition; fourth, attaining the virtues of the stage; and fifth, attaining meditative concentration.
Second, from "In the ocean of sentient beings" onwards is the benefit for others, consisting of two phrases:
the first establishes [the point], and the second explains it.
Third, from "Skillfully entering" onwards are two phrases concerning skillful entry into the Dharma-body: the first establishes [the point], and the second explains it.
The four lines beginning with "Pervasive Roaming" (遍遊) concern the birth of sentient beings in the Pure Land: first, the ocean of worlds; second, the ocean of lands.
The fourth, the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra, consists of four parts:

first, attaining the expedient means of all Buddhas across the three periods of time; second, discerning offerings; third, attaining the vows of Samantabhadra; and fourth, gathering and producing wisdom and virtue. These may also be correlated with the superior gathering of sentient beings.
Regarding the collection of conditioned causes (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya-samudaya*), the text contains thirty-three groups, with names listed from bottom to top.
The reason for this is to indicate the progressive increase and decrease [of the factors].
Question:
In which lands do these various assemblies dwell? Answer:
This assembly resides in one body within a single land; among the four lands, it occupies three lands and a portion of the transformation land—this is what should be reflected upon.
As for why the subsequent text praising the Buddha proceeds from top to bottom, it is to manifest the sequential order of the ranks of honor.
First, the assembly of *malla* wrestlers is divided into three parts:
first, the enumeration; second, the listing of names; and third, the praise of their virtues.
Regarding the praise of their virtues, the text consists of three sections:
The first is the general [section];
the next five lines are the specific [sections]:

1) the gate of possessing vows; 2) the gate of possessing virtues; 3) the gate of possessing meditative concentration; 4) the gate of possessing supernormal powers; and 5) the gate of possessing liberation—these constitute the virtues of self-benefit.
Third, the two lines beginning with "Abiding among all sentient beings" concern benefiting others.
The remaining assembly may be understood through their listed names and praised virtues.
As for the *garuḍa*, they are the golden-winged birds (*suparṇin*).
Kinnara: translated here as "Doubtful Deity," they perform music.
Mahoraga: translated here as "Mang Deity. Yama:
translated here as "Time Deity," also named "Sublime Goodness."
Tuṣita means "Contentment" in this [language].
Mahābrahmā means "One who has newly transcended the defilement of desire.
Maheśvara means "The Great Sovereign" (Mahādeva).
The text consists of three parts; the first two are readily understood.
Regarding the praise of his virtues, the text contains four sub-sections: first, a general praise;

second, a specific praise of his altruistic activity beginning with "toward all sentient beings"; third, a praise of his self-benefit beginning with "immeasurable exquisite forms"; and fourth, an explanation of the reasons why he accomplishes these two functions, beginning with "beholding the Buddha’s countenance" up to "for what reason? (so-yi-wei-he).
The third section concerns self-benefit, which is divided into three parts:

first, the body-action (*kāyakarman*) of the *dharmakāya* is explained; next, from "Among the ten powers" onwards, the mental action (*manaskarman*) is explained; and from "In the midst of all assemblies" onwards, the verbal action (*vākkarman*) is explained.
This passage consists of five statements, which can be understood through their sequential progression.
Regarding the reason for the fourth [statement], the text has two parts:
first, it clarifies that upon which it relies; second, it explains the reason why.
Therefore, regarding the middle section, there is first the question and then the answer.
The answer consists of three parts:

first, the clarification of the basis and object; second, from "In all Tathāgatas" onwards, the elucidation of how practice is accomplished based on that basis and object; and third, from "Each according to... onwards, the conclusion regarding the specific accomplishments and the attribution of merit to the Buddha.

The second passage contains six subordinate clauses: first, being in the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), one is gathered by the Buddha to cultivate roots of goodness; second, the Buddha leads one into the stage of understanding (*adhimukti*); third, having been gathered by the Buddha, one enters the stage of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*); fourth, from the phrase "attaining immeasurable merit" onwards, it clarifies the attainment of the effortless power (*anābhoga-vaśitā*) of the eighth stage and above; fifth, from the phrase "all are fully accomplished" onwards, it distinguishes the universal vows and practices (*samantabhadra-praṇidhāna-caryā*) of the ten stages and above.
Sixth, from "The Conduct of the Bodhisattva" onwards, the specific accomplishments are concluded.
Third, the conclusion that the merit resides in the Buddha; this section is divided into four parts: first, the conclusion [of the preceding];...
Second, the correct inference that the Tathāgata’s light of wisdom shines universally;
third, the attainment of the causal conditions, whereby one enters the ocean of the Buddha-fruit by means of the power of liberation, personally realizing the source [of this];
fourth, the attainment of mastery over the Dharma-gates, describing the fulfillment of one's own practice.
It may also be established through the successive analysis of the four propositions.
Next, regarding the passage praising the Buddha within the eighteen assemblies, this merely briefly indicates the hidden and the manifest from above; therefore, the eighteen are clarified.
This is divided into two main parts:
first, the Bodhisattvas such as Śubhavyūha each attain mastery over a single dharma-gate; second, the eighteenth, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, attains mastery over all dharma-gates.

In this context, one should reflect upon the scope of the section on the "gate of the shared and distinct births" as manifested through the analogy of a multi-storied pavilion of dependent origination.
Alternatively, it may be understood that the first seventeen are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the eighteenth, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, is their co-natal companion (*sahaja*).
Regarding ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there are seventeen textual sections.
Within the first, "The Excellence of the Ocean," there are two parts:
the first is the presentation of mastery over the gateways of the Dharma, which constitutes the offering performed through mental action (*manas-karman*).
The King’s own physical presence constitutes the offering of bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
Second, from the section on “Reciting Verses” (*gāthā*) onwards, the offering of verbal action (*vākkarman*) is distinguished.
The prose of these verses in total extols the Tathāgata’s fulfillment of the three types of action (*trikarman*) in their function of pervading the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Among these, the first six verses generally praise the superiority of the Buddha’s three karmas while remaining in the world;

the second section, beginning with "There are all sentient beings in the world," consists of six verses that describe the arising of extraordinary and sublime virtuous functions of the three karmas in the world;
next, the two verses beginning with "The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body" specifically praise his physical karma (kāyakarma).
Next, the two verses beginning with “The Tathāgata’s voice is unimpeded” separately praise the Buddha’s verbal activity;
next, the two verses beginning with “All the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions” distinguish the Buddha’s mental activity;
and the final two verses cite the causes to provide an explanatory proof.
Second, the section on the *Sukha-karma-prabhā* devas praising the Buddha’s virtue of the dual practice of tranquility and activity consists of three parts:

first, a general praise in one verse; second, sixteen verses that provide specific illustrations; and third, two verses beginning with "Innumerable and immeasurable kalpas" which cite the causes and bring the section to completion.
The third dhyāna contains seven verses on Pure Wisdom (*viśuddhajñāna*) and twenty-two stanzas that collectively praise the functional power of the Tathāgata’s bodily karma (*kāyakarman*).

The first six stanzas praise the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the next six praise the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); the following six praise the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*); and the final four stanzas collectively praise the Tathāgata’s virtue of compassion (*karuṇā*).
The ten days of the second dhyāna consist of twenty verses, which collectively praise the Buddha’s great practice of skillful means and the Dharma he has realized.

The first six verses collectively praise the Buddha’s practice of skillful means; the next six praise his gathering and transforming of beings through the gates of Dharma; the following six praise his transformation through the eight phases of attaining enlightenment; and the final two present the causes and provide a concluding summary.
The first dhyāna comprises ten verses. Within these, sixteen verses extol the Buddha’s qualities of tranquility, unimpededness, and mastery.

The first four verses praise the Buddha’s physical actions (kāyakarma); the next four praise the unimpeded nature of his verbal actions (vākkarma); the following four praise his mental actions (manaskarma); and the final four verses collectively praise the boundlessness of his three types of action.
The recitation text for the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations consists of twenty verses, which praise the function of the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

The first four verses praise the Dharmakāya for universally generating goodness and extinguishing evil; the next four praise the function of the Buddha’s vocal karma; the following two praise the function of his mental karma; the next six generally praise the Buddha’s ability to generate goodness and extinguish evil; and the final four praise the Buddha’s sovereign responsiveness to capacities without any sense of superiority.
Within the twenty verses concerning the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the virtues of the Buddha’s three bodies are praised:
the first six verses praise the sovereign power and function of the Dharmakāya, while the subsequent fourteen verses praise the Saṃbhogakāya.
The fourteen [verses] comprise four sections:

the first two distinguish the Buddha’s vocal karma; the next six, his bodily karma; the next four, praise the Buddha’s original causes; and the final two, praise the Buddha’s mastery in gathering in sentient beings.
In Tuṣita there are eight heavens; within these sixteen verses, the praise of the Buddha’s sovereign mastery in preaching the Dharma throughout the entire dharma-realm is summarized.

The first six verses generally praise the Buddha’s unimpeded functions; the next six praise the Buddha’s virtue of eliminating the three obstructions of birth; the following two praise the Buddha’s ability to accomplish the benefit of sentient beings’ practices so that it is not in vain; and the final two praise the perfect assembly of the multitude, manifesting the power of the Sage’s gathering.
The sixteen verses of the *Yāma* chapter collectively praise the meritorious qualities of the Buddha’s three types of action (*trikarma*).
The first eight concern mental action (*manaskarma*), the next two concern vocal action (*vākkarma*), and the final six concern physical action (*kāyakarma*).
The *Trāyastriṃśa* chapter consists of ten sections and twenty verses, collectively praising the gates of the provisional and ultimate bodhi-wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods.
The first four [sections] distinguish how those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha encounter sacred conditions;
the subsequent eight distinguish the Buddha’s skillful means for transforming sentient beings.
Next, six verses praise the Buddha’s attainment of the body of supreme wisdom, enabling those who enter this practice to achieve supreme benefit;
the final two verses conclude by exhorting mindfulness of the Buddha to extinguish the three obstacles, namely: afflictions, karma, and retribution.
There are ten "Suns" and twenty-two verses in total, collectively praising the merit of the Buddha’s wisdom-sun.

The first twelve verses praise the adornment of the Buddha’s manifold virtues; the next eight verses praise the Buddha’s supreme wisdom and skillful means; and the final two verses praise the profundity and vastness of the Dharma.

There are ten [verses] concerning the Moon Deity and sixteen in the verse; these collectively praise how the Buddha, amidst the darkness of ignorance, emits the light of wisdom and teaching to bring about the accomplishment of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
The first ten distinguish the benefits of the Buddha’s light of wisdom for the generation and realization of a mind that is unshakable;
