The eighth assembly, which was compiled after the [previous] meditative concentration, symbolizes the skillful means of knowledge that enables oneself and others to enter the *dharmadhātu*, rather than being intended to manifest the Dharma itself.
This may also serve to demonstrate that it includes the benefit of others rather than proving one's own thesis; it remains simply the Dharma being proven through the assembly of the multitude.

Second, regarding the identification of the distance from which the assembly has come—terms such as "ten," "hundred," or "thousand" are as they appear in the text—and other meanings are explained in accordance with the text.
The assembly of the multitude has four characteristics:

first, the place reveals the characteristics of the Dharma; second, the name of the Buddha manifests his understanding; third, the names of the bodhisattvas clarify the beginning and end of their stages; and fourth, the names of the seats distinguish the utility of the encompassing Dharma.
This refers specifically to newly ordained members of the assembly, whereas other cases apply universally.
Regarding the newly ordained members of the assembly from the ten directions, there are five textual sections:
first, the full assembly arrives here;...
Second, from "In this way, etc. onwards, is the summary;
third, from "The Bodhisattvas sit in succession" onwards, each reveals the Dharma-gates they have attained, manifesting their transformative virtue;
fourth, from "In every thought-moment, in each and every world" onwards, clarifies the sovereign power of dependent origination in transforming sentient beings.
The *Pañcavidyā* explains the verses. Within the first ten lines, each contains seven parts:

(1) the ocean location; (2) the Buddha-field; (3) the name of the Buddha; (4) the name of that bodhisattva by whom they were awakened to Buddhahood; (5) their arrival accompanied by an attendant; (6) the presentation of offerings to the Buddha; and (7) each sitting according to their original direction.

Regarding the second section of the text, concerning the arrival of ten billion bodhisattvas from ten billion buddha-fields and so forth: these are identical in essence as an ocean of lands and not distinct.

As for the fact that the names of these sentient beings' lands differ, it is to signify that while the fruit of their virtues is universally pervasive, the specific ways in which they gather and benefit beings within the present dharma vary.
The third section has six parts: first, having sat down;

second, light issuing from the pores; third, Bodhisattvas emerging from within the light; fourth, the Bodhisattvas' skillful means pervading all atoms; fifth, within each and every atom there is a Buddha-field; sixth, within each and every field a Buddha appears.
This is a matter of actual reality, not a provisional transformation.
The four subsequent passages consist of three parts:
first, the identification of those beings to be transformed;
Second, from "By means of the dharma-gate of mastery over dreams" onwards, the methods for transformation are distinguished, first through analysis and then by way of a conclusion;
third, from "In a single moment of thought" onwards, the benefits of the transformative manifestation are distinguished.
Regarding the benefits achieved, there are six phrases in the text: first, benefiting humans and devas;

second, benefiting those on the inner stages of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); third, benefiting those who have attained the ten stages of approach (*pratipannaka*) toward the fruits; fourth, benefiting those who have already completed the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*); fifth, benefiting those who have attained up to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*); and sixth, benefiting those who have attained the eighth stage and above.
The five verses consist of two parts:

the first ten stanzas praise the arrival of the bodhisattvas from the ten directions who have long cultivated sublime practices; the latter ten stanzas praise the preceding passages concerning their successive seating and their activities for the benefit of others.

The first ten [verses] are divided into three parts: the first two verses distinguish the Bodhisattva’s own virtues; the next five verses distinguish his ability to uproot birth and separate beings from suffering; the subsequent three verses demonstrate his extraordinary capacity by showing how, through the perfection of these virtues, he can travel everywhere to the abodes of the Buddhas of the ten directions; and the final ten verses generally summarize the textual passages concerning the Dharma-gates and the transformative virtues attained by those from the rank of "Great Seat" (mahāsattva) downward. The remaining characteristics may be understood accordingly.
Third, the Buddha manifests Samantabhadra to demonstrate that the one who preaches the Dharma should be respectfully invited by the assembly; this section consists of four parts:
first, distinguishing the purpose of emitting light;
second, the actual emission of light, which may be understood through five phrases.
The third is the correct manifestation where the three lights shine;
the fourth is the entry from beneath the feet, which signifies the gathering of functions back into their source and reveals the non-dual fusion of cause and effect.

Regarding the fourth [section], the emergence of the lotus and the bodhisattvas, there are three parts within the "Manifestation of the Ritual": 1. The emergence of the lotus. 2. The emergence of the bodhisattvas. 3. The manifestation of the ritual.
First, flowers emerge at the site of the assembly, which may also be the wheel-rim (*cakra*); this consists of seven phrases, revealing the scope of the gathering and transformation of beings.
Second, a great bodhisattva emerges from between the Buddha’s eyebrows, manifesting the teaching by means of persons.
Third, verses of praise are spoken, clarifying the scope of the teaching.
Regarding the second section, "The Bodhisattvas," there are seven parts:
first, the identification of the location;
second, the clarification of the individuals who appear there.
Third, the listing of names;
fourth, the retinue;
fifth, emerging and respectfully circumambulating their seats.
Sixth, there are two [points] regarding the withdrawal from one's seat;
seventh, from "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) onwards, there is praise for the virtues of the person who has emerged, consisting of four phrases.
The third verse consists of two [parts]:

First, Jin-yin (Victorious Sound) spoke six verses praising the Buddha’s transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and their mastery over the capacity of sentient beings as vessels for the Dharma, as well as manifesting the boundaries of the Dharma; this is the manifestation of the virtue of the teaching's sound.

Second, Shi-zi-yan-guang-fen-xun (Lion-Flame-Light-Vigorous-Pace) spoke seventeen verses, generally praising Vairocana and Samantabhadra for being able to equal all Buddhas and discerning the characteristics of turning the wheel of Dharma; this is the manifestation of the majesty of the teaching.
The first verse is divided into three parts:

the first two lines clarify the prior intention for the manifestation of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) pervading the dharma-realm; the next two lines clarify the extent of its manifested activity in preaching the Dharma and teaching; and the final two lines clarify its inconceivable majesty and power.
Within the verses of the second Bodhisattva, Vīryavega-svara, the first three distinguish the sovereign turning of the Dharma wheel by Vairocana;

the subsequent fourteen verses clarify the turning of the three karmas, which constitutes the "completeness of conditions. This explains how the three kinds of Dharma wheels are manifested in reliance upon conditions.
The initial passage consists of four parts:

first, the first half-verse provides a general manifestation; second, the second half-verse distinguishes the essence of the wheel; third, one line clarifies the directions and locations where it functions accordingly; and fourth, one line clarifies its characteristics and meanings.
The Wheel of Dharma has four kinds:
first, teaching; second, practice; third, principle; and fourth, activity.
Question:
How does this turning of the wheel of Dharma differ from the wheel of the three turnings and twelve aspects of the Three Vehicles? Answer:
This consists of a single turning that accomplishes its ten aspects; that is to say, it is a single turning of inexhaustible revolution, as explained in detail below.

Furthermore, the *Buddhacarita-sūtra* states: "Within the first fifteen days of the month of the lunar mansion Jyeṣṭhā, on the twelfth day, when the sun had passed its meridian and the shadows were difficult to overcome, the Buddha sat facing north; during the time of the lunar mansions Mūla and Rohiṇī, he turned the Brahma-wheel of Dharma."

Regarding the second section, the first six verses clarify the transformations of mental action (*manas-karman*); the next four verses distinguish the transformations of bodily action (*kāya-karman*); and the subsequent four verses distinguish the transformations of vocal action (*vāk-karman*).
Furthermore, there are seven explanations:

the first two generally distinguish the extent of the arising of transformations through cause and effect; the second pair distinguish bodily karma; the third pair clarify vocal karma; the fourth pair clarify mental karma; the next two pairs re-examine the boundaries of the body; the following two pairs re-examine the mouth; and the final two pairs re-examine the mind.
Second, the clarification of the essential nature of the samādhi section: this involves reverently receiving the Buddha’s power, being empowered to initiate [the practice].
Within this, there are two parts:
first, a detailed analysis according to the various assemblies; second, the explanation of the text.
The "Brief Analysis" is divided into four parts; this is the sixth section.

First, regarding existence and non-existence: entering meditative absorption serves to manifest the profundity of the Dharma, whereas the capacity of the audience in the second assembly alone was shallow, and thus the Dharma could not be profound for them.

Furthermore, because this abiding in skillful means lacks a substantial essence of its own stage, one does not enter meditative concentration; this is because the Dharma accords with the specific capacities of the audience.
Regarding the double entry and non-double entry: the meaning is repeated in the first assembly, whereas it is absent in the subsequent assemblies.

Furthermore, it may not be necessary to emphasize this point, as it is already explained within the context of the fundamental meditative absorption (samādhi); therefore, it is explained separately below.

Regarding the distinction between the essence of cause and effect: the first, seventh, and eighth [absorptions] clarify the meditative absorption of the Buddha, while the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth clarify the meditative absorption of the Bodhisattva.
As for what this means: first, because the stainless *tathāgatagarbha* is the pure essence, he enters the Samādhi of the Pure Treasury (*viśuddhagarbha*).
In the seventh assembly, because the practice for the fruit of self-benefit has matured, he enters the Samādhi of the Buddha-Flower Adornment (*buddhavaipulya*).
This statement refers to the Lord of Transformation (*nirmāṇādhipati*).

If we speak in terms of the practitioner, it is because they cultivate the cause for the *Avataṃsaka* fruit; since this cultivation begins from the very outset, the Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabha*) is emphasized.

In the eighth stage, the fruit of liberation within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the benefit of others is perfected; therefore, the Buddha himself enters the Lion’s Sport Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*), which likewise concerns the Lord of Transformation.
If we consider this in terms of practice, it represents the person who, by engaging with the objective realm, establishes their resolve and constructs the body [of realization].
Furthermore, since the dharmas revealed in these three assemblies pertain to both cause and fruit, they enter into the meditative absorption of the fruit.
The four intermediate assemblies involve entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*); these will be explained in accordance with the text.

Regarding the differences among those capable of entering: within the seven locations of entry into concentration, the first six assemblies clarify the entry of Bodhisattvas in order to manifest their partial accord with principle; they also clarify the individuals who experience exultation.

Regarding the eighth point, "the Buddha himself enters meditative absorption": this clarifies that the ultimate fruit-body of liberation within the *dharmadhātu* can be fully realized only by a Buddha; furthermore, it may serve to manifest the limit of phenomena (*dharmaparyanta*) by means of the Buddha, and also to reveal the scope of what is known by other beings in contrast to the Buddha.
The remaining points will be discussed below.
Next, following the text, the explanation is divided into three parts:
first, the analysis of Samantabhadra entering the Samādhi of the Pure Treasury;
Second, "illuminating all Buddhas without obstruction," wherein wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*) are divided into two;
third, from "having [attained] this" onwards, it distinguishes the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) attained equally by all Buddhas, which may also serve as a concluding summary.
Third, from "Entering this samādhi" onwards, the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is clarified; the text is divided into two parts:
first, a detailed analysis of the differences in the empowerments bestowed during the various assemblies, which constitutes the seventh section;
second, the explanation of the text itself.
There are two points for critical examination:
first, distinguishing between existence and non-existence; second, distinguishing the remoteness or proximity of the Buddhas, as well as the differences in their names and numbers.
Regarding existence and non-existence: in the second, seventh, and eighth assemblies, it is not clarified what the Buddhas add to [the teaching].

Bestowal generally functions as a fruit that provides benefit, enabling those in lower stations and possessing lower wisdom to gain strength, such that they are capable of expounding the higher Dharma and initiating superior progress.

Second, the analysis of the capacity: initially, it is indeterminate; to prevent both advancement and regression, one does not enter meditative absorption, thereby manifesting that the determination of the Dharma is profound.
Furthermore, because a person does not enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*) when clearly perceiving the Dharma, they do not apply [the antidotes].
There are two reasons for the seventh assembly:

first, because the basis upon which the practices of this assembly rely is no different from those of the preceding ones; second, to clarify that the coarse or subtle nature of the practitioner’s arising cultivation is indeterminate.

In the eighth assembly, it is explained that the Buddha himself enters samādhi; because the fruit of liberation within the dharma-realm is vast, perfect, and ultimate, there is no need for further empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Next, regarding the differences in the names of the Buddhas, these manifest the distinctions among their virtues.
Next, the explanation according to the text is divided into three parts:

first, the bestowal of oral empowerment (*vāg-adhiṣṭhāna*) and its purpose; second, from "At that time, all the Buddhas bestowed... onwards, the clarification of the bestowal of mental empowerment (*citta-adhiṣṭhāna*) and wisdom; third, from "At that time, in the ten directions... onwards, the clarification of the bestowal of physical empowerment (*kāya-adhiṣṭhāna*) by touching the crown of the head and granting fearlessness.
Furthermore, this passage is divided into two parts:
first, the explanation of the addition for the sake of entering meditative concentration;
second, from the words "That is to say" (*yad uta*) onwards, the explanation of the purpose of the addition, which constitutes the characteristics of the addition itself.
The initial section has three parts:

first, the manifestation of the bodies of all Buddhas for the sake of bestowing empowerment; second, from "Those Tathāgatas" onwards, the praise of the power to enter deep samādhi and the capacity to preach; third, from "All these" onwards, the clarification of the reasons for the empowerment and the praise.
The section on the enhancement of speech is divided into three parts:

first, a general overview; second, two lines that distinguish the essential nature of one's own and others' practices; and third, seven lines that clarify the functional application of altruistic practice.
The section on the enhancement of mind is also divided into three parts:

The first section provides a general overview, the second distinguishes the ten knowledges (daśajñāna) individually, and the third, beginning with "For what reason," provides the explanation and establishment.

Regarding the text on the initial ten knowledges: the first three pertain to self-benefit, while the latter seven pertain to the benefit of others; these are for the most part identical to the ten knowledges discussed below.

Why is it that, although the merit of the fruit has been described, the Buddha does not speak of it himself? This is to indicate that an inferior cause is capable of achieving a supreme fruit; furthermore, it is because Samantabhadra has attained meditative concentration, because he is the eldest son, because he is the leader of the assembly, because he has reached the depths of Vairocana Buddha’s vows, because of his original vow, and also because of the power of his own roots of goodness.

Following the preceding section, there should have been an account of [the Buddha] emerging immediately after bestowing the empowerment upon the crown of the head; however, that emergence is now omitted for brevity, as it is only explained at the beginning of the following section. The underlying intention can thus be understood.
Therefore, this clarifies that the various assemblies differ in their emergence from meditative absorption and their preaching of the Dharma; this is the eighth section.
First, the differences in emerging from absorption are distinguished.
The preaching of the Dharma in each assembly will be analyzed according to the respective texts.
The eighth assembly has entry but no exit, signifying that one enters the Dharma-realm without returning.
In the second assembly, both entry and exit are absent.

As for the first assembly, the text is not fixed; it may represent the simultaneous contemplation of the ultimate and conventional truths, or it may be due to a structural interweaving of the text; the remaining assemblies possess both entry and exit.
The fourth section consists of the Bodhisattvas’ collective re-requesting of Samantabhadra; this is the "Section on the Request.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, a brief prose passage expressing wonder that the intent has not been explained, which leads into the subsequent text of the request.

Samantabhadra was the first to request [the teaching], but it was requested by his own assembly alone; it was not requested by the combined assembly of both new and old followers. Because the request was incomplete, he did not preach it.
The request consists of twenty verses, divided into two parts:
first, the praise of virtues and the request; second, the final two verses which conclude the request.
The preceding text consists of five parts:

first, the initial two clarify that Samantabhadra has long cultivated various vows and practices under all Buddhas; since he should rely on these great vows to speak for the sake of the assembly, they are explained here.

Next, the following four clarify that Samantabhadra constantly perceives all Buddhas within the paths of the mundane world; since he should likewise manifest this for them to speak, it is now to be explained.

Next, the six [verses] distinguish how Samantabhadra, having long perfected the power of meditative concentration, universally knows the ocean of vessels and is able to preach extensively; they state that one should be like him and thus aspire to preach for the sake of the assembly.
Next, the four [verses] distinguish how Samantabhadra’s three karmas can rain down benefits for others; they ask why these are not preached.

Finally, the last two [verses] correctly identify the two lands—of nature and of retribution—as being attained through the cultivation of the ten powers, and exhort that they be preached according to the capacities of those present.
The following two sections constitute the request for instruction.

The reason why these requests for instruction are contained exclusively within the Ten Stages (Daśabhūmi) is that they serve as the causal evidence for the practice of the Dharma; other instances are not so.
